overview: This file traces the planning, construction, operation, and expansion of the Manchuria Chemical Industries Company’s chemical works at Dairen (modern Dalian) from 1932 through 1936. American consular reports describe the South Manchuria Railway Company’s decision to build an ammonium-sulfate plant in the Kwantung Leased Territory, its German technology and personnel, its closely guarded production methods, and suspicions that it could manufacture strategically useful chemicals such as ammonium nitrate and nitric acid. Later documents report the start of production, proposed aluminum sulfate, aluminum, caustic soda, and soda-ash facilities, and the rapid growth and geographical distribution of ammonium-sulfate exports, chiefly to Japan and Korea. Collectively, the papers place the enterprise within debates over Japanese-Manchukuo industrial relations, fertilizer markets, foreign machinery purchases, and preparations for war-related chemical production.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the proposed ammonium-sulfate plant at Dairen
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports confidentially the South Manchuria Railway Company’s decision to establish a large ammonium-sulfate plant at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Vincent reports a 90,000-ton ammonium-sulfate plant approved for Dairen, using Fushun coal dust, Japanese sulfur, and a Haber-like process; Baron Shiba wants confidentiality, framing the Kwantung site as avoiding Japan-Manchukuo competition disputes while mainly displacing British/German imports.

subfiles.title: Departmental abstract of the 1934 Dairen chemical-plant report
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Abstracts a voluntary Dairen report about the construction and possible military purpose of the Manchuria Chemical Industries plant.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Manchuria Chemical Industries' secretive Dairen plant, nominally for ammonium sulfate, is suspected of war-chemical production, employing 22 German engineers, mostly selling fertilizer in Japan.

subfiles.title: Voluntary report on Manchuria Chemical Industries at Ganjingzi
subfiles.from: Arnold Van Benschoten, American Vice Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Provides a detailed commercial and technical survey of the new Manchuria Chemical Industries plant at Ganjingzi near Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The report describes the company’s ownership, capitalization, construction, labor force, planned capacity, markets, prices, manufacturing process, raw materials, and machinery. It records strong indications that the works could manufacture ammonium nitrate and nitric acid, notes elaborate secrecy measures, and identifies twenty-two German engineers working in restricted sections. The plant was expected to use the German Uhde process, coal from Fushun, pyrites from Japan, and equipment sourced largely from Germany, while detailed compressor specifications document its high-pressure installation. The report also emphasizes the lack of a local fertilizer market and the likelihood that output would be sold in Japan, China, and other overseas markets.

subfiles.title: Departmental memorandum on the start of chemical production
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Dairen despatch reporting that the new ammonium-sulfate works had begun operating.
subfiles.summary: Memo reports the new Manchuria Chemical Industry plant produces ten tons hourly of ammonium sulfate, initially exported to Japan, planning South China/South Seas entry, plus aluminum sulfate and soda facilities.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the opening of the Ganjingzi ammonium-sulfate plant
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the start of production at Ganjingzi and related plans for aluminum, alum, caustic soda, and soda ash.
subfiles.summary: Grummon reports the Ganjingzi plant opened April 1935 at a third capacity, shipping its first 800 tons to Kobe; it planned naval-grade aluminum-sulfate production and soda facilities threatening British Imperial Chemical Industries' Mukden trade.

subfiles.title: Despatch on increased ammonium-sulfate output and exports
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes the rapid expansion of the Dairen plant’s ammonium-sulfate production and international exports.
subfiles.summary: Grummon shows Dairen ammonium-sulfate exports rose from 31,669 tons (1934) to 109,478 (1935), mostly to Japan with Korea/China gains and Hong Kong/Indies declines, discussing pricing and soybean-cake competition, and planning capacity to 240,000 tons.

interest: Shows a secretive Japanese-German chemical complex at Dairen, suspected of military purposes, transforming fertilizer exports.
